case_info.scenario: A 50-year-old woman presented to the dermatology department with a 10-year history of recurrent plaque outbreaks between her toes. She had a history of Bowen disease in the anus that had been treated with excision and skin grafting. Physical examination revealed multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes and on the vulva (Figure 1). Additionally, a 5 × 4 × 1-cm ulcerated perianal tumor with easy bleeding was noted. Coagulation, thyroid, liver, and kidney test results were within the normal ranges. Tests for syphilis, HIV, and autoantibodies were negative. However, the foot lesions were positive for human papillomavirus (HPV) 16, and the perianal, vulvar, and cervical lesions were positive for HPV-6, HPV-16, and HPV-18. A complete blood cell count revealed a decreased lymphocyte count of 400/μL (range, 1100-3200/μL; to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 0.001). The T-cell subset panel showed a total lymphocyte count of 564.45 cells/mL (range, 1200-3400 cells/mL) and a CD4+T-cell count of 59.95 cells/mL (range, 410-884 cells/mL).

options.B: Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma

case_info.answer: Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma
case_info.caption: Multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes.
case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. Immunomodulatory treatments such as IL-2 or antiretroviral therapy are also used, although their efficacy remains uncertain.7 Opportunistic infections are often quite similar in patients with ICL and in those who are HIV positive with low CD4+T-cell counts. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy is often prescribed for both, and regular monitoring of CD4+T cells and immune function guides treatment and helps to assess responses. Although no specific therapy for ICL exists, ongoing research is aimed at improving the understanding of this condition and development of additional treatment options. Meanwhile, the management of ICL emphasizes the prevention and treatment of infectious complications, similar to the management of HIV/AIDS.8 After diagnosis, the patient in the present case underwent surgical excision of the anal SCC and foot skin lesions and carbon dioxide laser treatment of the vulvar lesions. Later, she received 1 million units of pegylated subcutaneous IL-2 three times weekly. After 2 months of therapy, her CD4+T-cell count increased. She remains under close medical supervision.

The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. case_info.answer: Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma
case_info.caption: Multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes.
case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. Immunomodulatory treatments such as IL-2 or antiretroviral therapy are also used, although their efficacy remains uncertain.7 Opportunistic infections are often quite similar in patients with ICL and in those who are HIV positive with low CD4+T-cell counts. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy is often prescribed for both, and regular monitoring of CD4+T cells and immune function guides treatment and helps to assess responses. Although no specific therapy for ICL exists, ongoing research is aimed at improving the understanding of this condition and development of additional treatment options. Meanwhile, the management of ICL emphasizes the prevention and treatment of infectious complications, similar to the management of HIV/AIDS.8 After diagnosis, the patient in the present case underwent surgical excision of the anal SCC and foot skin lesions and carbon dioxide laser treatment of the vulvar lesions. Later, she received 1 million units of pegylated subcutaneous IL-2 three times weekly. After 2 months of therapy, her CD4+T-cell count increased. She remains under close medical supervision.

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."

case_info.answer: Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma
case_info.caption: Multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes.
case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. Immunomodulatory treatments such as IL-2 or antiretroviral therapy are also used, although their efficacy remains uncertain.7 Opportunistic infections are often quite similar in patients with ICL and in those who are HIV positive with low CD4+T-cell counts. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy is often prescribed for both, and regular monitoring of CD4+T cells and immune function guides treatment and helps to assess responses. Although no specific therapy for ICL exists, ongoing research is aimed at improving the understanding of this condition and development of additional treatment options. Meanwhile, the management of ICL emphasizes the prevention and treatment of infectious complications, similar to the management of HIV/AIDS.8 After diagnosis, the patient in the present case underwent surgical excision of the anal SCC and foot skin lesions and carbon dioxide laser treatment of the vulvar lesions. Later, she received 1 million units of pegylated subcutaneous IL-2 three times weekly. After 2 months of therapy, her CD4+T-cell count increased. She remains under close medical supervision.

case_info.answer: Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma
case_info.caption: Multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes.
case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. Immunomodulatory treatments such as IL-2 or antiretroviral therapy are also used, although their efficacy remains uncertain.7 Opportunistic infections are often quite similar in patients with ICL and in those who are HIV positive with low CD4+T-cell counts. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy is often prescribed for both, and regular monitoring of CD4+T cells and immune function guides treatment and helps to assess responses. Although no specific therapy for ICL exists, ongoing research is aimed at improving the understanding of this condition and development of additional treatment options. Meanwhile, the management of ICL emphasizes the prevention and treatment of infectious complications, similar to the management of HIV/AIDS.8 After diagnosis, the patient in the present case underwent surgical excision of the anal SCC and foot skin lesions and carbon dioxide laser treatment of the vulvar lesions. Later, she received 1 million units of pegylated subcutaneous IL-2 three times weekly. After 2 months of therapy, her CD4+T-cell count increased. She remains under close medical supervision.

case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. case_info.caption: Multiple dark brown, flat, hyperproliferative lesions with ulcerations and erosions located between the toes.
case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. Immunomodulatory treatments such as IL-2 or antiretroviral therapy are also used, although their efficacy remains uncertain.7 Opportunistic infections are often quite similar in patients with ICL and in those who are HIV positive with low CD4+T-cell counts. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy is often prescribed for both, and regular monitoring of CD4+T cells and immune function guides treatment and helps to assess responses. Although no specific therapy for ICL exists, ongoing research is aimed at improving the understanding of this condition and development of additional treatment options. Meanwhile, the management of ICL emphasizes the prevention and treatment of infectious complications, similar to the management of HIV/AIDS.8 After diagnosis, the patient in the present case underwent surgical excision of the anal SCC and foot skin lesions and carbon dioxide laser treatment of the vulvar lesions. Later, she received 1 million units of pegylated subcutaneous IL-2 three times weekly. After 2 months of therapy, her CD4+T-cell count increased. She remains under close medical supervision.

case_info.explanation: B. Idiopathic CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple squamous cell carcinoma Results of foot and vulva biopsies suggested squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in situ, and results of cervical biopsies suggested low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions. Biopsies of the anal lesion confirmed the presence of SCC (Figure 2). Therefore, the patient was diagnosed with CD4 lymphocytopenia with multiple SCC. Whole-exome sequencing did not reveal a monogenic cause but did revealCSF2andGSDMBgene variants, which are associated with an increased risk of HPV-associated cancers.1This observation suggested a genetic predisposition to the development of HPV-related cancers. The combination of genetic susceptibility, HPV infection, and CD4 lymphocytopenia likely created a permissive environment for the onset and recurrence of Bowen disease, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions in the cervix and vulva, and anal SCC. Idiopathic lymphocytopenia (ICL) is characterized by a CD4 lymphocyte count below 300 cells/mm3in the absence of any known primary or acquired cause of immunodeficiency. The clinical manifestations of ICL can vary from asymptomatic to severe complications that mimic the progression of AIDS. Immune deficiency is believed to play a pivotal role in ICL, and the degree of lymphopenia is often associated with overall disease severity.2 Opportunistic infections typically emerge when the absolute CD4+cell count drops below 200 cells/mm3. A diverse range of infections has been reported, including persistent genital infections from HPV, varicella-zoster virus, cryptococcal meningitis, mycobacterial infections,Fusobacterium nucleatum,Salmonella typhimuriumcausing sepsislike symptoms,Actinomycosisspecies,Rhodococcus equi, and cytomegalovirus retinitis.3 In addition to infectious diseases, ICL may be associated with some autoimmune conditions, such as systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, Sjögren syndrome, and psoriasis. The mechanisms that underlie the connection between ICL and autoimmune diseases are not completely understood but may involve dysregulation of the immune system.4 The ability to differentiate between HIV infection and ICL is critical. In contrast to HIV, in which CD4+cell counts decline rapidly over time, patients with ICL typically experience a slower decline, which may stabilize at a certain level. Additionally, patients with ICL usually do not show a rise in CD8+T lymphocytes, whereas these cells tend to increase early on in individuals with HIV as a response to the virus.5,6 The primary treatment for ICL involves prophylaxis and management of opportunistic infections, along with experimental strategies aimed at increasing CD4+T-cell counts. Immunomodulatory treatments such as IL-2 or antiretroviral therapy are also used, although their efficacy remains uncertain.7 Opportunistic infections are often quite similar in patients with ICL and in those who are HIV positive with low CD4+T-cell counts. Therefore, antimicrobial therapy is often prescribed for both, and regular monitoring of CD4+T cells and immune function guides treatment and helps to assess responses. Although no specific therapy for ICL exists, ongoing research is aimed at improving the understanding of this condition and development of additional treatment options. Meanwhile, the management of ICL emphasizes the prevention and treatment of infectious complications, similar to the management of HIV/AIDS.8 After diagnosis, the patient in the present case underwent surgical excision of the anal SCC and foot skin lesions and carbon dioxide laser treatment of the vulvar lesions.
